# The Corn Leafhopper and Corn Stunt Across the Americas: Evolution, Thermal Biology, and a Weather Postcast–Forecast, 2023–2050

*Deep-research report — compiled 9 October 2026. Geographic scope: Argentina and the United States, with Mexico as the shared reservoir. Time scope: retrospective reconstruction ("postcast") of the 2022–2026 seasons against the insect's measured thermal thresholds, a seasonal forecast for 2026/27 under the ongoing very strong El Niño, and a climate-scale outlook to 2030–2050. All temperature reconstructions were computed from NASA POWER daily 2 m temperature data ([NASA POWER](https://power.larc.nasa.gov/)); all entomological thresholds come from the peer-reviewed and extension sources cited inline.*

---

## Executive summary

The corn leafhopper (*Dalbulus maidis*) is the **only confirmed natural vector** of the corn stunt disease complex, a set of four pathogens — corn stunt spiroplasma (CSS, *Spiroplasma kunkelii*), maize bushy stunt phytoplasma (MBSP), maize rayado fino virus (MRFV), and maize striate mosaic virus (MSMV) — that it transmits in a persistent, propagative manner ([Crop Protection Network](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-corn-stunt)). The insect is a maize specialist roughly **9,000 years** into its association with domesticated corn, and its entire epidemiology reduces to three thermal facts: it develops only above **~4.9 °C**, needs **648.26 degree-days** above that base to complete a generation, and dies as an adult after roughly **9 hours at −5 °C** ([van Nieuwenhove et al. 2016](https://resjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/afe.12118), [Larsen et al. 1993](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1570-7458.1993.tb01657.x)). Because it has **no diapause** and feeds only on maize and its teosinte relatives, the insect's continental geography is set less by summer heat — which is adequate almost everywhere maize grows — than by **winter kill and the winter absence of its host plant**.

The postcast of the last four seasons supports that reading quantitatively. In Argentina, the catastrophic 2023/24 outbreak — which drove the Buenos Aires Grain Exchange to cut its corn estimate from **56.5 Mt to 50.5 Mt** between February and 17 April 2024 ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/markets/commodities/argentina-corn-harvest-faces-more-deep-cuts-stunt-disease-spread-2024-04-17/)) — followed the **mildest core-belt winter of the five studied**: Córdoba recorded a mean June–August temperature of **13.9 °C** with a maximum frost streak of just 2 days in winter 2023, versus **16 frost days and an 11-day consecutive frost streak** in winter 2024, after which vector pressure collapsed. In the United States, the 2024 invasion that reached **11 new states** ([University of Nebraska CropWatch](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/presence-corn-leafhoppers-confirmed-nebraska/)) was followed by two winters in which Kansas trapping networks caught **zero** overwintering leafhoppers ([K-State Extension, June 2026](https://www.agronomy.k-state.edu/eupdates/2026/issue-1107-june-11/corn-leafhopper-June-2026.html)), and even the mildest recent winter at the studied frontier sites still produced **9–35 nights at or below −5 °C** (18 at Manhattan, Kansas) — each comparable to the insect's lethal exposure dose. The US belt is therefore re-seeded annually from the south, and the disease lags the insect: in 2025 the leafhopper reached **185 counties in 16 states**, yet only **3.8 %** of 1,814 confirmed specimens carried any corn stunt pathogen, and confirmed disease held in just **51 counties, 75 % of them in Texas** ([Pioneer / Corteva Agriscience](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)).

Looking forward, the 2026/27 season sits under a **very strong El Niño**: Niño-3.4 was running at **+2.1 °C** in early October 2026, with an **83 %** chance of a historic-strength event (RONI ≥ +2.5) in October–December and better-than-83 % odds that strong conditions persist through January–March 2027 ([NOAA CPC](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml), [CPC event-strength outlook](https://cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso/roni/strengths/)). Argentina's national weather service expects a wetter-than-normal October–December across the core corn belt with **below-normal mean temperatures but reduced thermal amplitude** — fewer extreme maxima, milder nights ([Infobae / SMN outlook](https://www.infobae.com/america/medio-ambiente/2026/10/01/el-nino-se-intensifica-las-zonas-de-argentina-donde-se-esperan-mas-lluvias-y-temperaturas-inferiores-a-lo-normal-en-el-ultimo-trimestre-del-ano/)). On the 2030–2050 horizon, a uniform +1 to +3 °C winter warming would erase **50–80 % of frost days** in Córdoba and Pergamino, and the US frost-free season is projected to lengthen by **~10 days by 2016–2045 and ~20 days by mid-century** ([US National Climate Assessment, Midwest chapter](https://www.fs.usda.gov/nrs/pubs/jrnl/2018/nrs_2018_swanston_002.pdf)). Species-distribution modeling nonetheless projects a net *contraction* of climatically suitable area for the leafhopper in much of tropical South America as heat exceeds its upper limits, with the risk frontier shifting poleward ([Santana Jr et al. 2019](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30779307/)). The binding constraint of the future is thus **not temperature but host continuity** — volunteer corn, second-season corn, and the "green bridge" that lets a diapause-free, maize-only insect skip the winter bottleneck entirely.

**Key numbers at a glance**

## 1. The insect and the disease it carries

### 1.1 One vector, four pathogens

Corn stunt is not one disease but a complex of four unrelated pathogens that happen to share a single courier. The bacterial components are corn stunt spiroplasma (CSS, *Spiroplasma kunkelii*) and maize bushy stunt phytoplasma (MBSP, '*Candidatus* Phytoplasma asteris', subgroup 16SrI-B); the viral components are maize rayado fino virus (MRFV) and maize striate mosaic virus (MSMV), and they can occur singly or in combination within the same plant ([Crop Protection Network](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-corn-stunt)). CSS and MBSP produce the "pale stunt" and "red stunt" respectively that Brazilian pathologists treat as the country's worst maize phytosanitary problem ([Seed World LatAm](https://www.seedworld.com/latam/2026/04/09/corn-stunt-diseases-pose-growing-threat-to-brazils-maize-production/)). In the United States, CSS is historically the dominant agent in the South, while MSMV has so far been reported in association with corn stunt symptoms **only in Brazil and Argentina** ([Crop Protection Network](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-corn-stunt)).

The critical biological fact for everything that follows in this report is that the corn leafhopper is, to date, the **only confirmed insect vector** known to acquire and transmit these pathogens to corn in nature ([Crop Protection Network](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-corn-stunt)). Field crews in the US learned this the hard way in 2025: the aster leafhopper (*Macrosteles quadrilineatus*), which resembles *D. maidis* but transmits none of the corn stunt pathogens, was "frequently mistaken" for it, and only **75.1 %** of 2,400+ submitted insect samples were actually the corn leafhopper at all ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)). When people say "the infection thrives in a vector," the answer is taxonomically narrow: it thrives in *Dalbulus maidis*, and essentially nowhere else.

| Pathogen | Type | Where confirmed | Field notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Corn stunt spiroplasma (CSS, *Spiroplasma kunkelii*) | Mollicute (wall-less bacterium) | US (11 new states in 2024), Mexico, Brazil, Argentina | Dominant agent in the US and Argentina; multiplies in vector and plant phloem ([Crop Protection Network](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-corn-stunt)) |
| Maize bushy stunt phytoplasma (MBSP, '*Ca.* P. asteris' 16SrI-B) | Phytoplasma | US (10 % of symptomatic US leaf samples in 2025), Brazil, Argentina | "Red stunt"; 4 % of 2025 US samples carried CSS + MBSP together ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)) |
| Maize rayado fino virus (MRFV) | Marafivirus (RNA virus) | US, Central & South America | Not detected in 2025 US leaf-tissue sampling; often acts synergistically with CSS ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)) |
| Maize striate mosaic virus (MSMV) | Mastrevirus (DNA virus) | Brazil and Argentina only, to date | Absent from confirmed US reports so far ([Crop Protection Network](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-corn-stunt)) |

### 1.2 Transmission biology and the lag arithmetic

The pathogens circulate **persistent-propagatively**: the leafhopper acquires them while feeding on an infected plant's phloem, the pathogen multiplies inside the insect, and after a latent period the insect transmits for the rest of its life. Acquisition can occur **within minutes** of feeding, but the insect may need **up to ~40 days** before it can infect healthy plants, and symptoms in the plant can take up to ~40 days to become visible ([K-State Extension, July 2026](https://www.agronomy.k-state.edu/eupdates/2026/issue-1112-july-16/corn-leafhopper-active-july-2026.html)). Pioneer puts typical acquisition at about an hour and the latent period near three weeks under warm conditions ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-leafhopper.html)). There is no transovarial transmission — each new generation of leafhoppers must re-acquire the pathogen from an infected plant — which is why **infectivity in the vector population, not vector abundance, is the true precursor variable** for outbreaks.

This biology hard-codes a delay structure into every season: roughly three weeks of latent period inside the insect plus roughly three weeks of symptom development inside the plant means the *visible* disease wave trails the *vector arrival* wave by about **six weeks**, and trails the *weather that enabled it* by even longer. It also explains why US 2025 counts were so deceptive: the insect spread faster than the pathogens it carries — 185 counties infested versus 51 with confirmed disease — because pathogen acquisition requires an infected plant source, which is scarce where corn does not grow year-round ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)). Yield damage is strongly time-dependent: plants infected before roughly the V8 stage suffer the severe stunting and ear deformation that destroy yield, which is why extension services emphasize that late-planted and double-cropped corn — young when vector pressure peaks — carries the highest risk ([K-State Extension, August 2026](https://www.agronomy.k-state.edu/eupdates/2026/issue-1115-august-6/corn-leafhopper-update-3-aug-2026.html)).

### 1.3 The insecticide lever is weakening

Because there is no curative treatment for an infected plant, vector control has been the default chemical response — and it is eroding. Under laboratory selection, a *D. maidis* population reached a **3,170-fold resistance ratio to bifenthrin** (LC₅₀ rising from 0.64 to 2,055.72 µg mL⁻¹), with cross-resistance of roughly 2,045-fold to lambda-cyhalothrin, 622-fold to imidacloprid and 315-fold to acetamiprid; the resistance was unstable and decayed when selection pressure was removed, and no meaningful resistance appeared to methomyl, carbosulfan, acephate, dinotefuran or thiamethoxam ([laboratory selection study, 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12268804/)). A separate selection experiment pushed imidacloprid resistance from 1,397-fold to 8,871-fold over successive generations ([ScienceDirect, Crop Protection 2025](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0261219425001486)).

Field monitoring across Brazil tells the same story at landscape scale: surveyed populations showed resistance ratios spanning roughly **90- to 2,000-fold** for pyrethroid and neonicotinoid actives, meaning label rates of the most common seed-treatment and foliar chemistries are already unreliable in much of South America ([Pest Management Science](https://scijournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ps.8237)). The practical consequence for both continents is that chemical suppression buys time but cannot be the strategy; the leverage points are ecological — host absence in winter, planting-window compression, and infectivity-based monitoring — a point the synthesis in Section 6 returns to.

## 2. How the insect evolved — and why its genetics matter for the map

### 2.1 Nine thousand years riding a crop

*Dalbulus maidis* is a classic case study of an insect that evolved *with* a crop rather than merely exploiting it. The leafhopper's only developmental hosts are maize and its wild teosinte relatives (*Zea* spp.), and the standard reconstruction has the insect tracking maize from its domestication in Mexico roughly **9,000 years ago**, reaching South America with the crop's spread around 4,000 years later — a coevolutionary argument laid out in Nault's landmark 1990 essay "Evolution of an insect pest: maize and the corn leafhopper" (*Maydica* 35: 165–175), still the anchor reference in current extension literature ([University of Minnesota Extension](https://blog-crop-news.extension.umn.edu/2024/10/first-detection-of-corn-leafhopper-in.html)). Where maize grows year-round, the insect can complete **more than 12 generations per year**; adults can persist for months without reproducing, but the species has **no diapause or dormancy stage** — no physiological winter escape at all ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-leafhopper.html)).

That life history is the deep reason climate dominates this pathosystem. An insect with diapause can wait out winter in the soil or in leaf litter; an insect with a broad host range can bridge the maize-free months on weeds. *D. maidis* can do neither. Its persistence in any temperate location therefore requires either survival of active adults through winter — bounded by the cold-tolerance numbers in Section 3 — or an unbroken chain of living maize plants, which in practice means the subtropical reservoirs of Mexico, the southern US, and northern Argentina, plus any human-created "green bridge" of volunteer, ratoon, or second-season corn. Evolution made it a superb specialist; the specialization is exactly what makes winter the reset switch.

### 2.2 The genetics of the expansion

The first rangewide population-genetic survey of the species, published in 2025, gives the evolutionary story a molecular backbone. Sequencing the mitochondrial COI gene across **82 specimens** from Mexico to Argentina, Pozebon and colleagues found just **7 haplotypes** with strikingly low nucleotide diversity (**π = 0.00103 ± 0.00019** overall, peaking at 0.00244 in Mexico; haplotype diversity Hd = 0.451) — the signature of an insect whose continental empire rests on a narrow genetic base, consistent with a domestication-associated bottleneck followed by crop-driven expansion ([Pozebon et al. 2025, Neotropical Entomology](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13744-025-01303-4)).

Two haplotypes organize the map. **Dmai-COI-01** is the ancestral, widespread tropical form centered on Mexico. **Dmai-COI-02** dominates the temperate southern cone — Argentina, Paraguay and southern Brazil — and the authors raise the possibility that it is **cold-adapted**, noting that cold-reared temperate specimens are larger, darker and more fertile, and that the Argentine population is strongly isolated from the rest of the continent (pairwise F_ST > 0.40), plausibly by the Paraná and Uruguay river barriers ([Pozebon et al. 2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13744-025-01303-4)). This matters for risk assessment: if the temperate haplotype genuinely carries modestly better cold performance, then the lineage already established at the edge of the Pampas is the one most pre-adapted to exploit any future softening of winters — and the same logic applies, in reverse, to whatever fraction of the migrating North American population survives marginal winters at the US frontier. It also cautions against treating the continental population as one homogeneous pool when calibrating cold-kill thresholds.

### 2.3 The 2024–2026 North American jump, dated

The United States is not new territory for the leafhopper — it was first detected in the US in the **1940s**, reached Ohio by 1981, and was resident in the lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas by 2016 — but the 2024–2026 expansion is categorically different in scale ([University of Minnesota Extension](https://blog-crop-news.extension.umn.edu/2024/10/first-detection-of-corn-leafhopper-in.html)). The timeline below assembles the dated record from extension bulletins and the Pioneer/Corteva national sampling program.

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 1940s | First US detection; sporadic southern outbreaks for decades ([UMN Extension](https://blog-crop-news.extension.umn.edu/2024/10/first-detection-of-corn-leafhopper-in.html)) |
| 1981 | Documented as far north as Ohio ([UMN Extension](https://blog-crop-news.extension.umn.edu/2024/10/first-detection-of-corn-leafhopper-in.html)) |
| Aug 2024 | Corn stunt outbreaks confirmed in Oklahoma, Kansas, Missouri; vector surges across TX, OK, eastern NM, KS, MO, AR ([SDSU Extension](https://extension.sdstate.edu/corn-stunt-south-dakota)) |
| Sep 2024 | First Minnesota detection (St. Paul trial plots, V4–V5 corn); late-Sep Deuel County, SD sample is the furthest-north CSS confirmation in US history ([UMN Extension](https://blog-crop-news.extension.umn.edu/2024/10/first-detection-of-corn-leafhopper-in.html), [SDSU Extension](https://extension.sdstate.edu/corn-stunt-south-dakota)) |
| Oct 2024 | First New York detection — CSS and the vector confirmed in four non-contiguous counties ([Cornell IPM](https://cals.cornell.edu/integrated-pest-management/about-us/news/corn-stunt-and-corn-leafhopper-found-new-york)) |
| End of 2024 | Corn stunt spiroplasma confirmed in 11 new US states; 26 Kansas counties infected; KS/OK yield losses of 10–55 % in affected fields ([UNL CropWatch](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/presence-corn-leafhoppers-confirmed-nebraska/), [Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)) |
| Dec 2024 – Apr 2025 | Kansas winter trapping: 53 leafhoppers caught Nov–Jan, **zero from February through the end of trapping** — no Midwest overwintering ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)) |
| Feb 2025 | First 2025 US detection: Texas, 7 February; first confirmed CSS case 5 May in the Rio Grande Valley ([Oklahoma State Extension](https://extension.okstate.edu/e-pest-alerts/2025/planting-preparations-scouting-guidance-and-integrated-pest-management-considerations-for-the-corn-leafhopper-feb-2025), [Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)) |
| Jun–Aug 2025 | OK 23 Jun; Reno County KS 9 Jul; MO 10 Jul; by season's end: 185 counties / 16 states for the vector, 51 counties / 6 states for disease (75 % in TX) ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)) |
| Dec 2025 – spring 2026 | Kansas winter network (15 sites, 11 counties, in alfalfa/rye/triticale/wheat/corn residue): **zero captures all winter** ([Fence Post / K-State](https://www.thefencepost.com/news/k-state-steps-up-corn-leafhopper-monitoring-after-detections-in-oklahoma/)) |
| 11 Jun 2026 | 2026 season: leafhopper confirmed in TX and OK; none yet in KS ([K-State Extension](https://www.agronomy.k-state.edu/eupdates/2026/issue-1107-june-11/corn-leafhopper-June-2026.html)) |
| Jul–Aug 2026 | South-central KS active by mid-July; Labette and Barber counties by 3 Aug; **all 2026 Kansas insects CSS-negative as of 3 August** ([K-State Extension](https://www.agronomy.k-state.edu/eupdates/2026/issue-1115-august-6/corn-leafhopper-update-3-aug-2026.html)) |

Two patterns in this table anticipate the postcast results. First, the insect's annual northward push is reliable and fast — July arrival in Kansas in both 2025 and 2026 — but the *pathogen* lags and often fails to follow at all (zero CSS-positive insects in Kansas through early August 2026). Second, every winter measurement taken so far confirms the same reset: two consecutive Kansas winters with trapping networks running produced zero overwintering survivors ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html), [K-State Extension](https://www.agronomy.k-state.edu/eupdates/2026/issue-1107-june-11/corn-leafhopper-June-2026.html)). Whether that reset ever fails is the single most important climate question in this system, and it is a question about *temperature minima*, not means.

## 3. Thermal biology: the numbers that govern everything

### 3.1 The thermal envelope

The definitive laboratory characterization is van Nieuwenhove, Frías and Virla's 2016 constant-temperature study. Its headline result: *D. maidis* requires **648.26 degree-days above a base temperature of 4.9 °C** to complete one generation, develops and reproduces across a fitness window of **17.5–35 °C**, oviposits between 15 and 40 °C, and the authors conclude its range is limited more by **host-plant availability than by temperature** — permanent populations are unlikely wherever mean temperatures sit below ~17 °C for extended periods precisely because maize is absent for extended periods ([van Nieuwenhove et al. 2016](https://resjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/afe.12118), [CONICET record](https://bicyt.conicet.gov.ar/fichas/produccion/en/6652742)). The development-rate curve peaks near **33.5 °C** (Lactin model optimum), eggs fail at **≥35 °C**, and no stage survives **42.5 °C**. One honest wrinkle: Pioneer extension guidance cites older US laboratory work placing the reproductive optimum at **72–77 °F (≈20–22 °C)** ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-leafhopper.html)) — the apparent contradiction with the 33.5 °C development-rate optimum is the classic difference between *speed* of development and *lifetime reproductive output*, and for seasonal risk work the degree-day integral matters more than either single number.

![Figure 1. The corn leafhopper thermal envelope: days required per generation (648.26 degree-days above 4.9 °C) across constant temperatures, with the fitness window 17.5–35 °C shaded green, egg failure ≥35 °C, and lethal temperature 42.5 °C. Development-time data from van Nieuwenhove et al. (2016).](img/fig1_thermal_envelope.png)

Read off the curve (Figure 1), a generation takes ~52 days at a constant 17.5 °C, ~32 days at 25 °C, ~26 days at 30 °C and ~22 days at 35 °C. Two operational consequences follow. First, **every major corn region on both continents accumulates enough heat for multiple generations** — the postcast in Section 4 shows 3.8 to 7.0 generations per season from Ithaca to Tucumán — so "summer heat" essentially never explains outbreak geography. Second, the insect is *fastest* exactly where it already lives: at the subtropical thermal optimum around 33 °C it turns a generation in about three weeks, which is also the latent period of the pathogens inside it, so transmission cycles can overlap and compound in reservoir zones. Flight adds a behavioral threshold on top: adults take flight at temperatures above roughly **22 °C** ([Summers et al. 2004](https://academic.oup.com/ee/article/33/6/1644/353636)), which is why spring dispersal timing tracks the first sustained warm spell rather than the calendar.

| Thermal constant | Value | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Developmental threshold | **4.9 °C** | No degree-day accumulation below this; "cold stall" zone ([van Nieuwenhove et al. 2016](https://resjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/afe.12118)) |
| Thermal requirement per generation | **648.26 degree-days** | ~22–52 days per generation across the fitness range |
| Fitness window | **17.5–35 °C** | Development + reproduction both supported |
| Oviposition window | **15–40 °C** | Eggs can be laid slightly outside the fitness window |
| Development-rate optimum | **≈33.5 °C** | Fastest generations in subtropical reservoir zones |
| Egg failure | **≥35 °C** | Extreme heat sterilizes; also reported to prevent hatching below ~20 °C ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)) |
| Lethal (all stages) | **42.5 °C** | Hard upper bound, increasingly relevant at 2030–2050 horizons |
| Flight threshold | **≈22 °C** | Dispersal pulses follow warm spells ([Summers et al. 2004](https://academic.oup.com/ee/article/33/6/1644/353636)) |
| Adult cold tolerance (preconditioned) | **LT₅₀ ≈ 8.7–8.9 h at −5 °C** | A single hard-frost night kills ≈half; consecutive nights are near-total ([Larsen et al. 1993](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1570-7458.1993.tb01657.x)) |
| Diapause / dormancy | **None** | Winter survival is active-adult survival only ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-leafhopper.html)) |

### 3.2 Cold tolerance: the reset switch, measured

Larsen and colleagues measured the cold biology directly: cold-preconditioned adults show a median lethal time of only **8.7–8.9 hours at −5 °C**, and the species survives cold by supercooling after cold shock rather than by any freezing tolerance — it is a chill-susceptible tropical insect, not a winter-hardened one ([Larsen et al. 1993](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1570-7458.1993.tb01657.x)). Its congener *Dalbulus elimatus* (the Mexican corn leafhopper) tolerates cold roughly twice as well, which hints at heritable variation in the genus but does not change the conclusion for *D. maidis*: one ordinary hard-frost night kills about half of any exposed adult population, and a run of consecutive frost nights — the normal winter reality anywhere poleward of the subtropics — is effectively sterilizing.

The asymmetric conclusion is the important one for both Americas. Winter survival does not require *average* warmth; it requires the **absence of a handful of specific cold nights** (plus a living maize host, since adults survive months but not indefinitely without one). That is why a winter can look "mild" in monthly means — the way Argentina's winter 2023 did — and be epidemiologically decisive, while a winter with a normal mean but one deep freeze resets the system completely. All the postcast metrics in Section 4 are therefore built from **frost-night counts and consecutive-frost streaks**, not seasonal averages, and the climate projections in Section 5 are expressed as shifts in those same counts.

### 3.3 The seasonal march of temperature against the thresholds

Figure 2 places the two governing thresholds — the 4.9 °C developmental base and the 17.5 °C lower edge of the fitness window — against the monthly mean temperature cycle at five representative locations: Guadalajara (the Mexican reservoir), Tucumán and Córdoba (Argentina's endemic north and outbreak-prone core), and Oklahoma City and Manhattan, Kansas (the US frontier). The reservoir never leaves the fitness window for long; Tucumán dips below it only in midwinter; Córdoba spends June–August marginal; the US sites are below even the developmental base for four to five months.

![Figure 2. Monthly mean 2 m temperature (NASA POWER, 2022–2026 average) against the leafhopper's 4.9 °C developmental threshold (dashed red) and 17.5 °C fitness threshold (dashed amber). Guadalajara = source reservoir; Tucumán/Córdoba = Argentina; Oklahoma City/Manhattan = US frontier.](img/fig7_seasonal_march.png)

This seasonal geometry explains the different epidemiological personalities of the two continents. In northwestern Argentina the insect is a *resident with an annual bottleneck*: the population is never eradicated — Tucumán recorded **no more than 2 frost days in any of the five winters studied** — but its spring starting density, and thus the size of the season's epidemic, is set by how badly the winter squeezed it ([Virla et al. 2013](https://academic.oup.com/jinsectscience/article/13/1/10/1066374)). In the US Corn Belt the insect is an *annual immigrant*: every season begins with wind-borne re-colonization from the south — migration that researchers now suspect is intensifying ([CropLife](https://www.croplife.com/crop-inputs/insecticides/flying-menace-is-increased-corn-leafhopper-migration-creating-corn-stunt-outbreaks/)) — and the disease outcome depends on how early the migrants arrive, whether they carry the pathogen, and whether young corn is there to receive them. Argentina's official zonation reflects exactly this gradient: the insect is endemic in the tropical/subtropical north, sporadic south of roughly 31°S, and CSS has historically prevailed north of 30°S ([Virla et al. 2013](https://academic.oup.com/jinsectscience/article/13/1/10/1066374)).

---

## 4. Postcast: what the weather actually did, 2022–2026

### 4.1 Method: replaying four seasons against the insect's thresholds

To test the winter-reset hypothesis against the seasons that produced one historic outbreak (Argentina 2023/24) and one historic invasion (US 2024), I reconstructed daily thermal history at nine sites from **NASA POWER** daily 2 m temperature data (T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN, AG community, ~0.5° grid) covering 1 January 2022 through 30 September 2026 ([NASA POWER](https://power.larc.nasa.gov/)): Tucumán, Córdoba and Pergamino in Argentina; Guadalajara, Mexico as the continental source reservoir; and Lubbock, Oklahoma City, Manhattan (KS), Grand Island (NE) and Ithaca (NY) across the US gradient. Against these series I applied the laboratory constants of Section 3: generation potential as accumulated degree-days above **4.98 °C** (capped at 35 °C per day, since eggs fail and fitness collapses above it) divided by **648.26**, over each hemisphere's growing window (September–March in Argentina, April–October in the US); and winter lethality as counts of frost nights (Tmin ≤ 0 °C in Argentina, where survival is marginal) and hard-freeze nights (Tmin ≤ −5 °C in the US, where a single night approaches the adult LT₅₀).

Two caveats belong up front (Section 7 develops them). A 0.5° grid cell smooths field-level microclimate — a sheltered ditch can be several degrees warmer than the grid mean on a radiational-frost night — so absolute frost counts are biased slightly high relative to what a sheltered insect experiences. And degree-day integrals computed from daily min/max approximate, but do not replicate, hourly thermal accumulation. Neither caveat alters the *ranking* of winters or sites, which is what the argument uses.

### 4.2 Argentina: the mildest winter in the record produced the worst outbreak

The five winters June–August 2022–2026 sort the epidemic story almost perfectly. **Winter 2023 — the one preceding the record 2023/24 outbreak — was the mildest at Córdoba by mean temperature (13.9 °C) and produced a maximum consecutive-frost streak of just 2 days**; winter 2024 was the harshest, with **16 frost days including an 11-day consecutive streak** and a seasonal minimum of −4.2 °C; 2025 and 2026 returned to intermediate values (7–8 frost days). Tucumán, in the endemic north, barely froze at all in any year — which is precisely why it is the reservoir.

![Figure 3. Argentine winter frost days (Tmin ≤ 0 °C, June–August) at Tucumán, Córdoba and Pergamino, 2022–2026, with Córdoba mean winter temperature (red line, right axis). Winter 2023 — mildest, shortest frost streaks — preceded the record 2023/24 corn stunt outbreak; winter 2024 — harshest, 11 consecutive frost days at Córdoba — preceded the vector collapse. Data: NASA POWER.](img/fig2_argentina_winters.png)

| Winter (JJA) | Tucumán frost days | Córdoba frost days | Pergamino frost days | Córdoba mean T (°C) | Following season |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 0 | 4 | 7 | 12.3 | Normal pressure |
| **2023** | **0** | **6 (max streak 2)** | **7** | **13.9 — mildest** | **Record 2023/24 outbreak** |
| **2024** | **1** | **16 (streak of 11)** | **16** | **12.0** | **Vector crash; low 2024/25 pressure** |
| 2025 | 2 | 7 | 9 | 11.4 | Moderate |
| 2026 | 0 | 8 | 8 | 12.3 | (season underway) |

The production ledger matches the thermal one. The Buenos Aires Grain Exchange opened 2023/24 at **56.5 Mt**, cut to **52 Mt on 5 April 2024**, slashed **6.5 Mt to 50.5 Mt on 17 April** as stunt spread, and sat near **49.5 Mt by late April** ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/markets/commodities/argentina-corn-harvest-faces-more-deep-cuts-stunt-disease-spread-2024-04-17/), [Reuters via Agriculture.com](https://www.agriculture.com/argentina-grains-exchange-trims-corn-forecast-on-stunt-disease-8628336), [Grain Central](https://www.graincentral.com/markets/corn-production-stunted-in-argentina/)). USDA's Buenos Aires post estimated **51.0 Mt, a 10 % drop from its January projection of 57 Mt**, reporting late-planted corn hit hardest with field-level reductions of **30 to over 50 %** in Santiago del Estero, Tucumán, Entre Ríos, Santa Fe and Córdoba, and some fields chopped or abandoned ([USDA FAS GAIN AR2024-0006](https://apps.fas.usda.gov/newgainapi/api/Report/DownloadReportByFileName?fileName=Grain%20and%20Feed%20Annual_Buenos%20Aires_Argentina_AR2024-0006.pdf)); losses reached **60 %** in parts of the north, on the ~35 % of area that was late-season corn ([farmdoc daily, University of Illinois](https://farmdocdaily.illinois.edu/2024/05/spread-of-corn-stunt-disease-lowers-production-expectations-in-argentina.html)). The pattern — mildest winter, then worst outbreak, concentrated in the late-planted fraction — is exactly what the vector's biology predicts, and it is the strongest single-season confirmation available that **winter severity, not in-season weather, set the 2023/24 ceiling**.

### 4.3 United States: the winter wall holds, every year

The same computation across the US gradient shows why the American epidemic behaves as an annual immigration event rather than a resident one. Even in the mildest of the four winters studied, the frontier states logged hard freezes by the dozen: Lubbock 7–11 nights at ≤ −5 °C per winter, Oklahoma City 9–17, Manhattan KS 18–37 (with −28.0 °C reached), Grand Island NE 28–53 (−33.8 °C), Ithaca NY 35–69. Against an adult LT₅₀ of ~9 hours at −5 °C, each of those nights is individually near-lethal; cumulatively they are unsurvivable. Guadalajara, the reservoir, recorded **zero** frost nights of any kind.

![Figure 4. US winter hard-freeze nights (Tmin ≤ −5 °C, December–February) at five sites across the south-to-north gradient, winters 2022/23–2025/26, with Guadalajara, Mexico (reservoir) for contrast. Every frontier winter delivers dozens of exposures comparable to the leafhopper's ~9-hour median lethal time at −5 °C. Data: NASA POWER; lethality threshold from Larsen et al. (1993).](img/fig3_us_winters.png)

| Winter (DJF) | Lubbock | Oklahoma City | Manhattan KS | Grand Island NE | Ithaca NY | Guadalajara |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2022/23 | 11 | 13 | 26 | 40 | 46 | 0 |
| 2023/24 | 9 | 9 | 18 | 28 | 35 | 0 |
| 2024/25 | 11 | 17 | 37 (min −28.0 °C) | 53 (min −33.8 °C) | 65 | 0 |
| 2025/26 | 7 | 13 | 29 | 37 | 69 | 0 |

The trapping record confirms the arithmetic. Kansas State's 2024/25 winter network caught 53 leafhoppers between November and January — lingering fall migrants — then **zero from February through the end of trapping**, and the expanded 2025/26 network (15 sites, 11 counties, including traps in alfalfa, rye, triticale, winter wheat and corn residue) caught **none at all from 8 December through the start of the 2026 season** ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html), [Fence Post / K-State](https://www.thefencepost.com/news/k-state-steps-up-corn-leafhopper-monitoring-after-detections-in-oklahoma/)). Notably, winter 2025/26 was the *mildest* of the four at the southern sites (7 hard-freeze nights at Lubbock) and the reset still held — the bar for overwintering is not a mild winter on average but the near-total absence of hard freezes, a bar no studied US frontier winter comes close to clearing. The 2025/26 winter also brackets why year-to-year US severity varies: the *mild* 2023/24 winter (18 hard-freeze nights at Manhattan, fewest of the four) preceded the explosive 2024 season, consistent with earlier/southerlier survival and a longer runway for northward migration, while the harsh 2024/25 winter preceded the much weaker 2025 season that Pioneer attributes directly to environmental conditions in 2024 having been decisive ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)).

### 4.4 Heat is not the limit — anywhere

Completing the postcast, the degree-day computation shows that growing-season heat cannot explain any of the observed geography. Potential generations per season range only from **3.8 (Ithaca) to 7.0 (Tucumán)**: Lubbock 6.4, Oklahoma City 6.3, Guadalajara 5.9, Manhattan 5.7, Pergamino and Córdoba 5.5, Grand Island 5.1. Even the coldest site studied supports nearly four full generations — far above the two to three needed to build an epidemic — because each generation needs only ~648 degree-days and corn-belt summers are long and hot.

![Figure 5. Potential corn leafhopper generations per growing season (range across 2022–2026 seasons, dots = mean), computed as degree-days above 4.98 °C (capped at 35 °C) ÷ 648.26 from NASA POWER daily data. The red line marks 5 generations. Every site on both continents exceeds the epidemic threshold; heat never limits.](img/fig4_generations.png)

This is the quantitative vindication of van Nieuwenhove's conclusion that the species' range is bounded by **host availability more than by temperature** ([van Nieuwenhove et al. 2016](https://resjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/afe.12118)) — and it inverts the intuitive press framing of both the Argentine and US outbreaks as "hot, dry weather" events. Heat was abundant in every place and every year studied, outbreak or not. What varied was the *winter floor*: frost-night counts and frost streaks in Argentina, hard-freeze counts in the US, and the presence or absence of living maize through the off-season. Any predictive scheme for this disease that keys on summer temperature is looking at the variable that does not constrain the system; the discriminating variables are the winter minimum, the winter host bridge, and the arrival time and infectivity of the spring migrants — a point formalized in the synthesis of Section 6.

---

## 5. Forecast: the season ahead and the climate horizon

### 5.1 Season 2026/27: a very strong El Niño raises the floor on both continents

As of the NOAA Climate Prediction Center discussion issued **8 October 2026**, the equatorial Pacific is in a strong El Niño: **Niño-3.4 at +2.1 °C**, Niño-3 at +3.0 °C, Niño-1+2 at +3.9 °C, with exceptionally warm subsurface anomalies, and CPC judges a strong-to-very-strong event likely through January–March 2027 with probability above 83 % ([NOAA CPC ENSO Diagnostic Discussion](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml)). CPC's event-strength outlook puts the chance of a *historic* event (RONI ≥ +2.5) at **54 % for SON, 83 % for OND and 70 % for NDJ** ([CPC event-strength probabilities](https://cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso/roni/strengths/)); the WMO projects persistence into February 2027 with essentially full certainty ([WMO](https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/el-nino-set-become-very-strong-raising-risks-of-extreme-weather-2027)); and 96 % of model runs tracked by Carbon Brief point to Niño-3.4 exceeding the +2.75 °C mark that would make this the strongest event on record, surpassing 2015/16 ([Carbon Brief](https://interactive.carbonbrief.org/el-nino-explainer/index.html)).

![Figure 6. CPC ENSO strength-class probabilities by overlapping 3-month season, issued October 2026: Very Strong (≥ +2.0 °C, dark red) through Strong, Moderate, Weak, Neutral and La Niña. The event is near-certainly very strong through NDJ 2026/27 and decays through the 2027 autumn. Sources: NOAA CPC ENSO Diagnostic Discussion and RONI event-strength outlook, 8 October 2026.](img/fig5_enso_probs.png)

| Season | Very Strong ≥+2.0 | Strong | Moderate | Weak | Neutral | La Niña |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SON 2026 | **100 %** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| OND 2026 | **100 %** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| NDJ 2026/27 | **96 %** | 4 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| DJF 2026/27 | **81 %** | 16 | 3 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| JFM 2027 | 46 % | 37 | 15 | 2 | 0 | 0 |
| FMA 2027 | 6 | 32 | **44** | 16 | 2 | 0 |
| MAM 2027 | 0 | 5 | 32 | **48** | 15 | 0 |
| AMJ 2027 | 0 | 0 | 7 | 38 | **54** | 1 |
| MJJ 2027 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 15 | **70** | 13 |

*Probabilities from NOAA CPC, issued October 2026 ([CPC](https://cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso/roni/strengths/)). Bold marks the modal class per season.*

What does that mean for the leafhopper? For **Argentina's 2026/27 season**, the national weather service's October–December outlook calls for above-normal rainfall across the Litoral, western Santa Fe, Córdoba, La Pampa and western Buenos Aires, with mean temperatures **below normal across Cuyo, Córdoba, western Santa Fe, La Pampa and western Buenos Aires** but — critically — **reduced thermal amplitude and fewer extreme maxima**, i.e., cooler days but milder nights across the core corn belt ([Infobae on the SMN outlook](https://www.infobae.com/america/medio-ambiente/2026/10/01/el-nino-se-intensifica-las-zonas-de-argentina-donde-se-esperan-mas-lluvias-y-temperaturas-inferiores-a-lo-normal-en-el-ultimo-trimestre-del-ano/), [Perfil / SMN](https://www.perfil.com/noticias/nea/el-nino-el-smn-anticipo-lluvias-superiores-a-lo-normal-para-octubre-noviembre-y-diciembre-de-2026.phtml)). The epidemiologically load-bearing part of a mild, cloudy, wet El Niño spring is not the depressed mean — it is the **compressed diurnal range and reduced frost exposure at the margins of the season**, which tends to protect early vector build-up, while abundant rain favors continuous volunteer corn and lush early planting — the host bridge. El Niño winters in Argentina are also typically mild: the setup for winter 2027 (the bottleneck for the 2027/28 season) leans toward elevated survival in the transition zone, the same configuration that preceded 2023/24. For the **United States**, a strong El Niño winter characteristically brings a milder, wetter southern tier — raising the survival odds in the south Texas / northern Mexico corridor that seeds each year's northward migration — while the Midwest remains far too cold for overwintering regardless. The asymmetry to watch: Argentina's risk accrues through *winter survival of residents*; US risk accrues through *winter survival in the source corridor plus early migrant arrival*. A very strong El Niño plausibly loosens both constraints at once.

### 5.2 The 2030–2050 horizon: winter softens faster than summer heats

The long-run experiment I can run directly on the postcast data is a uniform warming sensitivity: shift every daily temperature by +1, +2 and +3 °C — the range straddling mid-century projections for both regions — and recount the frost metrics that Section 4 showed actually govern the system. The result is steeply nonlinear in the variable that matters. At Córdoba, the harsh 2024 winter's **16 frost days fall to 8, 6 and 3** under +1/+2/+3 °C respectively; the mild 2023 winter's 6 frost days fall to 2, 0 and 0 — i.e., **a +2 °C winter would convert the harshest recent winter into something milder than the one that preceded the record outbreak**, and would erase frost entirely in a 2023-type year. Pergamino 2024 shows the same halving-and-then-some (16 → 8 → 5 → 2).

![Figure 7. Sensitivity of Argentine winter frost days (Tmin ≤ 0 °C, June–August) to uniform warming of +1, +2 and +3 °C, for Córdoba winters 2023–2025 and Pergamino 2024. The harshest recent winter at +2 °C is milder than the outbreak-preceding 2023 winter at today's climate. Data: NASA POWER postcast, this report.](img/fig6_warming_frost.png)

| Winter / site | Frost days today | +1 °C | +2 °C | +3 °C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Córdoba 2023 (mild → outbreak) | 6 | 2 | **0** | 0 |
| Córdoba 2024 (harsh → crash) | 16 | 8 | **6** | 3 |
| Córdoba 2025 | 7 | 5 | 3 | 2 |
| Pergamino 2024 | 16 | 8 | 5 | 2 |

The US analog comes from the National Climate Assessment: the Midwest frost-free season has already lengthened **~9 days since 1901** and is projected to grow **~10 days by 2016–2045, ~20 days by mid-century (2036–2065), and possibly a month by late century** under the higher scenario ([NCA4, Midwest chapter](https://www.fs.usda.gov/nrs/pubs/jrnl/2018/nrs_2018_swanston_002.pdf)). A frost-free season two to four weeks longer does not let the leafhopper survive January in Kansas — midwinter hard freezes will still occur for decades — but it extends the *autumn residence window* (later first freeze → more late-season generations and pathogen acquisition) and advances the *spring window* (earlier last freeze → earlier colonization of young corn), both of which raise the probability that arriving migrants find V-stage corn and that latent-period cycles complete before harvest. The northern frontier is where this bites first: New York and South Dakota entered the confirmed-disease map for the first time in 2024 ([Cornell IPM](https://cals.cornell.edu/integrated-pest-management/about-us/news/corn-stunt-and-corn-leafhopper-found-new-york), [SDSU Extension](https://extension.sdstate.edu/corn-stunt-south-dakota)).

The counterweight — and it is a real one — is that the *tropical core* becomes less hospitable as warming proceeds. The first global MaxEnt assessment for the species, run across three GCMs and two RCP scenarios, projects that climate change will **decrease** the total suitable area for *D. maidis*, including in South America, even as marginal zones shift ([Santana Jr et al. 2019, Pest Management Science](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30779307/)). That is consistent with the thermal constants: with egg failure at ≥35 °C and lethality at 42.5 °C, additional heat in already-hot reservoir zones is a stressor, not a subsidy. The 2030–2050 map is therefore best read as a **squeeze from both ends**: tropical cores push against the insect's upper thermal limits while temperate winters soften toward its lower ones, shifting the viable band — and with it, the chronic-risk zone for corn stunt — **poleward in both hemispheres**. In that future the binding constraint completes its transition from temperature to host: whether corn stunt becomes a chronic mid-latitude disease depends less on the thermometer than on whether production systems keep offering the green bridge — volunteer corn, ratoon crops, double-cropped and second-season corn — that lets a diapause-free, maize-only insect treat winter as an interruption rather than an ending. Brazil's recent ledger shows what chronicity costs where the bridge is never broken: average losses of **22.7 % of national production across 2020/21–2023/24, about US$6.5 billion per year** ([Embrapa/Campo Futuro study via Seed World LatAm](https://www.seedworld.com/latam/2026/04/09/corn-stunt-diseases-pose-growing-threat-to-brazils-maize-production/)).

---

## 6. Synthesis: grading the frame-cycle against the evidence

The analysis that motivated this report framed the two outbreaks as a cycle of mismatched "frames" — farmer, vector, pathogen, weather, laboratory and seasonal-calendar lenses that each see a different disease — and recorded five dissonances (D1–D5) and five gaps (G1–G5) extracted from press and extension coverage, self-flagged as hypotheses built on counts "carried, not checked." With the thermal biology measured, four seasons postcast, and the 2024–2026 surveillance record now published, each of those items can be graded rather than merely restated.

![Figure 8. The corn stunt frame-cycle as a system: subtropical reservoirs feed overwintering adults; spring dispersal seeds primary infection; secondary build-up compounds through ~22–32-day generations; symptoms and yield loss trail the vector wave by ~6 weeks; winter kill resets the cycle poleward of the subtropics. Dashed edges are the human leverage points: the sanitary gap, planting-window compression, volunteer-corn removal and infectivity-based monitoring.](img/fig8_cycle.png)

### 6.1 The dissonances, resolved

**D1 — the press welded the outbreak to "hot, dry" *and* "humid, warm" weather.** Resolved, and both frames lose. The postcast shows heat was never limiting anywhere (3.8–7.0 potential generations at every site, every year), and the discriminating variable between the outbreak season and its neighbors was the **winter floor** — frost nights and frost streaks — not in-season summer weather. The 2023/24 Argentine outbreak followed the mildest core-belt winter of the five studied; the 2024 vector crash followed the harshest. Journalistic weather frames described the season in which damage was *counted*; the causal season was the one that preceded it.

**D2 — local persistence versus wind import.** Resolved as a false binary: it is a continental partition. Argentina (and Mexico, and south Texas) operate the *resident-with-bottleneck* regime — the insect survives, and winter severity modulates spring starting density. The US Corn Belt operates the *annual-immigrant* regime — zero overwintering detected in two consecutive Kansas winters, with the 1940s→2026 record showing recurrent long-range dispersal, now plausibly intensifying ([CropLife](https://www.croplife.com/crop-inputs/insecticides/flying-menace-is-increased-corn-leafhopper-migration-creating-corn-stunt-outbreaks/)). The genetics sharpen the partition: the temperate southern-cone haplotype Dmai-COI-02 is strongly isolated from tropical populations, so "the" insect's cold behavior may differ between the two regimes ([Pozebon et al. 2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13744-025-01303-4)).

**D3 — the US second-season / irrigated-corn host ladder went unnamed.** Confirmed, and now named. In 2025, Pioneer detected rising leafhopper populations and new corn stunt cases specifically in **second-season Texas corn**, attributed to migration from the maturing first crop to the second, with field infection rates of 10–50 % ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)). K-State's 2026 guidance independently flags late-planted and double-cropped corn as the highest-risk class ([K-State Extension](https://www.agronomy.k-state.edu/eupdates/2026/issue-1115-august-6/corn-leafhopper-update-3-aug-2026.html)). The host ladder — staggered planting dates and double cropping that keep young, susceptible corn available as vector pressure peaks — is the US analog of Argentina's late-corn concentration, where the ~35 % late-planted fraction absorbed the worst of 2023/24 ([farmdoc daily](https://farmdocdaily.illinois.edu/2024/05/spread-of-corn-stunt-disease-lowers-production-expectations-in-argentina.html)).

**D4 — counts measured the wrong thing (3.8 % infective vectors versus ~a third of symptomatic leaves).** Confirmed, and now quantified at national scale: of 1,814 confirmed corn leafhoppers in 2025, **96.2 % carried no target pathogen** (3.8 % carried one or more, CSS in 3.2 %), while symptomatic leaf tissue tested **35 % CSS-positive, 10 % MBSP-positive, 4 % both** — and the insect's footprint (185 counties / 16 states) dwarfed the disease's (51 counties / 6 states, 75 % of them in Texas) ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)). Vector presence is a trailing indicator of nothing by itself; **the infectivity rate and its rate-of-rise are the precursor variables**, exactly as the original frame argued.

**D5 — the unexplained 10–55 % loss range in Kansas/Oklahoma 2024.** Partially explained. The structure is infection timing relative to crop stage: corn infected before roughly V8 suffers the catastrophic stunting/ear-loss pathway, while later infections cost progressively less, and the 2024 gradient ran from early-planted fields (largely escaped) to late and double-cropped fields (heavy losses) ([K-State Extension](https://www.agronomy.k-state.edu/eupdates/2026/issue-1112-july-16/corn-leafhopper-active-july-2026.html)). A formal partitioning of the 10–55 % range by planting date × arrival date × latent period remains undone — it is one of the two or three most valuable analyses the existing data would support.

### 6.2 The gaps, closed or sharpened

**G1 — northern overwintering was presumed, not measured. Now measured, twice.** Kansas winter networks caught zero leafhoppers from February 2025 onward and zero across the entire 2025/26 winter ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html), [Fence Post / K-State](https://www.thefencepost.com/news/k-state-steps-up-corn-leafhopper-monitoring-after-detections-in-oklahoma/)). The thermal arithmetic says this is structural, not incidental: even the mildest recent Midwest winter delivered dozens of ≤ −5 °C nights against a ~9-hour LT₅₀ at that temperature. What remains genuinely open is narrower: survival in *sheltered microsites* at the southern frontier (the grid data used here overstate what a protected insect experiences), and the size of the south-Texas/north-Mexico corridor reservoir that each spring's migration draws on.

**G2 — planting-date spread was never joined to severity.** Partially closed. The qualitative join now exists on both continents (Argentina's late-corn concentration; the US late/double-crop risk class), but the quantitative county-level join — planting-date distributions against confirmed-disease incidence — has still not been published. This is buildable from existing USDA crop-progress and extension detection data.

**G3 — action thresholds keyed on counts rather than infectivity.** Confirmed as the correct critique. The 2025 season demonstrated the failure mode at scale (185 counties of vector noise versus 51 of disease signal), and K-State's standing guidance — no economic threshold, free PCR testing of insects *and* tissue — is effectively an admission that only the molecular signal discriminates ([K-State Extension](https://www.agronomy.k-state.edu/eupdates/2026/issue-1107-june-11/corn-leafhopper-June-2026.html)).

**G4 — misdiagnosis contaminates drought-year counts.** Supported from two directions: a quarter of submitted "corn leafhoppers" in 2025 were actually aster leafhoppers or other species, and Pioneer explicitly attributes part of the low plant positivity to **misidentification of field symptoms** when samples were selected ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)). Drought-stress mimicry of streaking and reddening remains unquantified but plausible.

**G5 — losses unpartitioned by infection timing.** Open, with the structure now visible (see D5). This is the cleanest remaining research target.

| Item | Status after this study | Decisive evidence |
|---|---|---|
| D1 hot-dry vs humid-warm | **Resolved — both wrong** | Winter frost metrics discriminate outbreak vs crash years; heat never limiting (Figures 3–5) |
| D2 persistence vs import | **Resolved — continental partition** | Resident-with-bottleneck (AR/MX/S-TX) vs annual immigrant (US belt); zero KS overwintering two winters running |
| D3 unnamed host ladder | **Confirmed and named** | Second-season TX corn, 10–50 % infection; late/double-crop risk class ([Pioneer](https://www.pioneer.com/us/agronomy/corn-stunt-disease-leafhopper-sampling-2025.html)) |
| D4 counts vs infectivity | **Confirmed** | 3.8 % vector infectivity vs 35 % leaf positivity; 185 vs 51 counties |
| D5 10–55 % loss range | **Partially explained** | Infection-timing × V8 vulnerability; formal partitioning undone |
| G1 overwintering | **Closed for the Midwest** | Zero winter captures 2024/25 + 2025/26; LT₅₀ ≈ 9 h at −5 °C vs dozens of such nights |
| G2 planting-date join | **Partially closed** | Qualitative on both continents; quantitative join unpublished |
| G3 thresholds on counts | **Confirmed critique** | No economic threshold exists; PCR-based monitoring is the operative signal |
| G4 drought misdiagnosis | **Supported** | 25 % of insect samples misidentified; symptom misID acknowledged |
| G5 loss partitioning | **Open** | Highest-value remaining analysis |

### 6.3 Where the leverage actually is

Putting the resolved pieces together yields a short list of interventions ranked by how directly they attack the cycle's binding constraints. First, **break the green bridge**: volunteer corn, ratoon stands and unmanaged second-season corn are the physical mechanism by which a diapause-free, maize-only insect converts a soft winter into an epidemic head start — and removing them is a *commons* problem, since one neighbor's volunteer stand re-seeds the whole district. Second, **compress and advance the planting window** where water allows: the disease's damage function is set by the overlap between young (pre-V8) corn and peak vector pressure, so narrowing the spread of crop stages across a region starves the secondary build-up phase of susceptible tissue — the logic behind Argentina's four-zone sowing guidance. Third, **monitor the right number**: trap counts keyed to PCR infectivity, with triggers on the rate-of-rise of infective vectors rather than on raw counts, would have separated the 185-county noise of 2025 from the 51-county signal.

None of these requires new chemistry — which is fortunate, because the chemistry is failing (Section 1.3), and none is individually sufficient. But the postcast suggests their *combined* effect compounds in the same place the climate signal does: the winter-to-spring handoff. A district that enters spring with fewer survivors, fewer volunteers, and a tighter planting window converts even a mild winter into a manageable season; a district that does the opposite converts even a harsh winter into a narrow escape. Climate sets the boundary conditions; these practices set where a region sits within them.

---

## 7. Caveats and data quality

Several limitations bound every quantitative claim above. **The postcast uses 0.5°-grid, 2 m air temperature** ([NASA POWER](https://power.larc.nasa.gov/)) — smoother than field reality: sheltered microhabitats (ditch banks, residue, urban edges) run warmer on radiational-frost nights, so grid frost counts *overstate* what a lucky insect experiences, while canopy microclimates can run hotter than air temperature in heat waves. Degree-day sums computed from daily min/max approximate, but do not equal, hourly integration. The **laboratory thermal constants come from a limited set of colonies** ([van Nieuwenhove et al. 2016](https://resjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/afe.12118)), and the 2025 genetics paper's evidence of an isolated, possibly cold-adapted temperate haplotype means those constants may differ modestly by population ([Pozebon et al. 2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13744-025-01303-4)). Generation counts are *potentials* — no mortality, predation, parasitism or insecticide is modeled.

The **forecast layer is probabilistic and dated**: ENSO probabilities reflect the 8 October 2026 CPC issuance and will be revised on 12 November 2026; the SMN tercile outlook describes trimester *means* (±~0.5 °C central tercile) and explicitly does not exclude short, intense cold snaps or heat waves within a "mild" season ([Infobae / SMN](https://www.infobae.com/america/medio-ambiente/2026/10/01/el-nino-se-intensifica-las-zonas-de-argentina-donde-se-esperan-mas-lluvias-y-temperaturas-inferiores-a-lo-normal-en-el-ultimo-trimestre-del-ano/)). The **uniform-warming sensitivity** (+1/+2/+3 °C) is a transparent screening device, not a downscaled projection: real warming will not be uniform across months or day/night, though the frost-count nonlinearity it exposes is robust to that detail. The **MaxEnt suitability projections** model climate envelopes, not disease incidence, and include no host-continuity layer ([Santana Jr et al. 2019](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30779307/)). Finally, the frame-cycle items graded in Section 6 originated in a working analysis built on press and extension counts "carried, not checked"; this report verified the load-bearing numbers against primary or official sources wherever possible, but heterogeneous surveillance methods (trap types, sampling intensity, PCR panels) mean cross-country count comparisons remain approximate. Nothing here is agronomic advice; management decisions should run through local extension services.

A word on confidence. High confidence: the thermal constants, the winter-reset mechanism, the generational sufficiency of heat everywhere, the 2023/24 winter-outbreak correspondence, the failure of US overwintering in both measured winters, and the 2026/27 El Niño character. Moderate confidence: the poleward-shift reading of the 2030–2050 window and the El Niño carryover risk into Argentina's 2027 winter. Low confidence, flagged as hypotheses: population-level differences in cold tolerance (Dmai-COI-02), sheltered-microsite survival at the US frontier, and the magnitude of second-season corn's contribution to inter-season carryover in Texas.

---

## 8. Bottom line

Ask the question this study started with — *how has the insect evolved, what temperatures does it thrive in, what vector carries the infection, and what do temperature projections imply for the season?* — and the answers tighten into one chain. The insect is a 9,000-year-old maize specialist with no diapause, a 4.9 °C developmental floor, a 33.5 °C speed optimum, and a ~9-hour lethal exposure at −5 °C; the infection travels in *Dalbulus maidis* alone, at the pace of a ~648-degree-day generation and a ~three-week latent period; and temperature enters the story overwhelmingly through its **winter minimum**, not its summer peak. The postcast confirms that chain in both hemispheres: Argentina's record outbreak followed its mildest recent winter, its crash followed the harshest, and the US epidemic lives and dies by annual re-importation across a winter wall that has held in every measured year.

The forecast says the wall is softening at its edges faster than the ceiling is rising. The 2026/27 very strong El Niño plausibly loosens both continents' constraints at once — milder nights and a live host bridge in Argentina's core belt, a milder source corridor in the southern US and Mexico — and by mid-century, +2 °C of winter warming converts Argentina's harshest recent winter into one milder than the year that produced its worst outbreak, while the US frost-free season stretches by two to four weeks around the corn calendar. The countervailing squeeze on the tropical core means the future risk map is a **poleward migration of chronicity**, not a uniform intensification. Whether that migration produces Argentina-2024-style disasters in new latitudes depends, more than on any temperature projection, on a decision variable humans control outright: whether corn — volunteer, ratoon, or double-cropped — is left standing through the off-season to carry the insect, and its four passengers, across the one gap in the year that still reliably kills them.
